turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's a pleasure to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Yeah, nice to meet you too. Well, I guess what brings me in today is... man, it's just been really frustrating at work lately. I'm a supervisor for a sales team—not retail, you know, outside sales—and there's just a ton of tracking and reporting I have to handle to keep everything running smoothly. 

But the thing is, I just keep making these really, really dumb mistakes on the sales reports. It's driving me absolutely crazy. I'll be sitting there at my desk, looking at the team dashboard to pull our weekly metrics, and I'll just copy the wrong numbers down. Like, I'll look right at the screen and somehow type something completely different into my spreadsheet, or I'll put a guy's stats in the wrong row entirely. 

And it happens with our standard operating procedures, too. I'll be going through a compliance checklist or an approval process that I'm supposed to verify, and I'll just completely miss a line in a procedure I was supposed to check. Just skip right past it. The most frustrating part—and this is what really made me realize I needed to come talk to somebody about this—is that I *do* check my work. I swear, I will sit there and look over the whole document, and I'll think I went over it perfectly. I'll tell myself, "Alright, looks good," and send it off, and then my boss will email me back ten minutes later pointing out a glaring error. I just don't understand how I can look right at it, think I've thoroughly reviewed it, and still miss these obvious details. It's making me look really careless to upper management, and I just... I don't know, it's exhausting.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless mistakes, such as copying wrong numbers and missing lines in procedures, despite attempting to check their work.

turns.doctor_question: Have you struggled with this kind of difficulty staying focused or being detail-oriented your whole life, or is this a relatively new problem for you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man, no, it's definitely not new. Not at all. I mean, if you ask my mom, she'll tell you it's been going on pretty much since day one. Actually, she still brings it up, which, you know, is a whole other thing, but she kept all these old report cards and teacher notes from back when I was in elementary school. She's got this whole box of them in her attic. 

And it's funny—well, maybe not funny, but looking back, it's exactly the same kind of stuff I'm dealing with now. The teachers were always writing these long notes home saying how I rushed through all my classwork just to get it done, completely missing half the instructions. And the homework... I don't even know how many times I lost my homework. I would literally do it sitting right there at the kitchen table with her watching me, and then by the time I got to school the next morning, it was just gone. Vanished into thin air. 

And it wasn't just the work, either. The notes were always complaining that I was talking out of turn, interrupting the teacher, blurting things out in the middle of a lesson... and I just could not stay in my seat to save my life. They'd have to remind me over and over and over again to just sit down. I'd be up wandering around, going to the pencil sharpener for the fifth time, looking out the window, whatever. So yeah, I was absolutely like this as a kid, too. It's just that now, you know, there's actual money and my career on the line instead of just a sticker on a spelling test, so the stakes are way higher. But the actual things I'm struggling with? Yeah, it's the exact same as when I was eight years old.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes rushing through classwork and missing instructions, indicating careless mistakes and inattention to detail.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports frequently losing their homework between doing it at home and arriving at school.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states they could not stay in their seat during class and would wander around the room.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient mentions a history of blurting things out in the middle of lessons.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient describes talking out of turn and interrupting the teacher.

turns.doctor_question: Do you still find yourself struggling with that same level of physical restlessness or need to be moving around now, as an adult, in your day-to-day life?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yeah, it hasn't gone away at all, it just... looks a little different now that I'm an adult, I guess. Like, I'm not wandering over to the pencil sharpener in the middle of a lesson anymore, obviously, but the actual physical feeling is exactly the same. 

We have these long meetings at work—these quarterly forecasting meetings, or sometimes just the weekly pipeline reviews with the whole team—and sitting through them is just... man, it's actual torture. Sitting through a long meeting feels like my body is literally buzzing inside. Like there's this electric hum right under my skin, and it just builds and builds the longer I have to sit still. I'll be in that conference room, and after maybe fifteen or twenty minutes, I'm just constantly shifting around in my chair. I'll cross my legs, uncross them, lean forward, lean back, adjust my collar. 

I'll start tapping my foot, too, which actually got me in a really awkward spot a couple of weeks ago because I guess I was bouncing my heel so hard I was shaking the conference table, and the regional director actually stopped talking and looked right at me. It was mortifying. But I just can't help it! I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until someone looks at me. 

And when the shifting and the tapping isn't enough, I literally have to make up an excuse to get up. I'll drink like three huge cups of coffee before we start just so I have a legitimate biological reason to excuse myself to the restroom. Or I'll stand up and go over to the whiteboard to draw a chart, even if I don't really need to write anything down, just to stretch my legs. Or I'll offer to go grab water bottles for the room. I'm always the guy volunteering to run to the kitchen during long sessions, and everyone thinks I'm just being this great, attentive host for the team, but the truth is I just desperately need to walk down the hall. Because if I stay in that chair for one more minute with that buzzing feeling, I feel like I'm going to jump out of my own skin. So yeah, the restlessness is definitely still there, it's just something I have to constantly manage and hide so I don't look like a crazy person in front of my reps.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes constantly shifting in his chair, crossing and uncrossing his legs, and tapping his foot or bouncing his heel during meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states he frequently makes up excuses to leave his seat during long meetings, such as going to the restroom, drawing on the whiteboard, or fetching water.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms ongoing restlessness, describing an internal 'buzzing' sensation and feeling like he will jump out of his skin if forced to sit still.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the physical restlessness, do you still find yourself frequently interrupting others or blurting out your thoughts before someone else has finished speaking?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah. Yeah, definitely. That is... honestly, that might be one of the things that gets me into the most trouble at work, aside from the reporting errors. It's just a constant thing, especially in meetings. 

I do it all the time with my reps. We'll be in a team huddle, or even just on a quick one-on-one call, and someone will start talking—maybe asking a question about a client, or bringing up an issue with a pitch—and they'll get maybe five or six words out, and my brain just instantly jumps ahead. I hear the start of the sentence and I just assume I know exactly where they're going with it. So I jump in before they can even finish talking. 

I'm really not trying to be rude or talk over anybody, I swear. In my head, it feels like I'm being efficient, you know? Like, "Okay, I see the problem, boom, here's the solution, let's keep things moving." But then... well, then they just stop talking and look at me kind of weird, and I'll realize that I completely cut them off and, worse, I answered the totally wrong point. Like, they'll say, "Actually, I was going to ask about the shipping logistics, not the pricing." And I just feel like an idiot. 

Just last week, I did it with the regional director. He was trying to explain this new territory alignment, and I interrupted him probably three times because I kept thinking he was leading up to a point about our quarterly quotas. I just blurted out my thoughts right over him. He actually had to hold up his hand—like, physically put his hand up to stop me—and say, "Just let me finish." It was so embarrassing. But it's like the words are just right there on the tip of my tongue, and if I don't get them out that exact second, I'm going to explode. I just fast-forward the whole conversation in my head and respond to the fast-forwarded part instead of actually waiting to hear what the person is trying to say. It makes people think I don't care about what they're saying, which really isn't true at all, I just... I can't seem to put the brakes on and just let them get to the end of their own thought.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient mentions getting into trouble at work for 'reporting errors', indicating careless mistakes.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they jump in and blurt out answers before people finish talking, often answering the wrong point.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient describes constantly interrupting others, cutting them off, and talking over them in conversations and meetings.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the careless mistakes and missing details in your work, do you find that you also frequently lose items like your keys, phone, or wallet, or do you often struggle to keep your mind on a task for more than a few minutes at a time?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man, the losing things... it's a nightmare. It is an absolute, daily nightmare. I am constantly—and I mean literally constantly—hunting for my phone, or my keys, or my work badge. It's like I set things down and they just cease to exist in my reality until I spend twenty minutes tearing my house or my office apart. 

Just... just the other day, for example, I was walking into the office, right? And I had my keys in one hand, my phone in the other, and this manila folder with the weekly call logs that I *just* had in my hand. I remember having it. I walked past the breakroom, maybe stopped for thirty seconds to pour a cup of coffee, and when I got to the conference room... the folder was gone. Just gone. I had to retrace my steps, checking the counter, checking the hallway, checking the printer room even though I hadn't even gone in there. 

And that's the worst part, really, because it gets so incredibly embarrassing when my reps are waiting on me to start a meeting. They'll be sitting there in the conference room, all logged in and ready to go, and I'm practically sprinting up and down the hallway patting my pockets, looking for my badge so I can get back into my own office to find the phone I left on my desk. They're all just looking at their watches, and I'm sweating, trying to laugh it off like, "Oh, Monday mornings, am I right?" but it's Tuesday, or it's Thursday, and it happens all the time. 

I'll have a pen, I'll set it down, it vanishes. I'll have my phone, I'll put it in my jacket, but I forgot I took my jacket off, so I actually left it on the hood of my car. It's just... it's exhausting, honestly, having to retrace my steps fifty times a day just to function. My wife is always saying I need a 'launch pad' by the door, like a special bowl for my keys, but I'll just put my keys next to the bowl, or I'll take them out of the bowl to check the mail and then leave them inside the mailbox. It never ends. So, yeah, to answer your question, keeping track of my stuff is a huge, huge problem for me. It's like my brain just deletes the memory of where I put my hands the second I let go of something.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly and extensively describes constantly losing everyday items like their phone, keys, work badge, and folders, which causes significant disruption and embarrassment.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find that these same struggles with focus, restlessness, and impulsivity follow you home and impact your personal life and relationships as much as they do your professional life?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man, yeah. It's... it's everywhere, honestly. It doesn't just clock out at five o'clock when I leave the office. It's like this shadow that just follows me around no matter where I am or who I'm with. 

Actually, at work, it's gotten to the point where I can't really just laugh it off or hide behind my sales numbers anymore. Just last month, my manager actually put it in my formal review. Yeah, a formal, written performance review. I was sitting in his office, and he slides this document across the desk, and right there under the 'Areas for Improvement' section is this whole detailed paragraph about my lack of attention to detail, how I'm disruptive in team settings, how I'm constantly dropping the ball on administrative stuff. It was... man, it was a massive gut punch, you know? Because I work so hard, I really do, but seeing it in black and white like that, knowing it's officially on my HR record... it just makes you feel like you're completely failing, despite trying so hard to keep all the plates spinning. 

And then I go home, hoping to just decompress, but it just bleeds right into my personal life, too. It adds to so much conflict at home. My wife, she's a saint, she really is, but I can see how exhausted she gets with me. Because I'll promise to do things—like, I'll look her right in the eye in the morning and say, "Yes, I will absolutely pick up the dry cleaning on the way home," or "I'm going to fix that broken drawer in the kitchen tonight." And I mean it! In that moment, I entirely intend to do it. But then the day happens, and my brain is jumping in a million directions, and I just completely forget. Or I'll actually start the project, take the drawer apart, and then get distracted by something in the garage, and leave my tools all over the kitchen counter for three days. 

And it just builds up. It causes so many arguments because people in my life just feel like they can't count on me to follow through on anything. That's the exact phrase my wife used the other night when we were arguing about me forgetting to pay the water bill—"I just can't count on you." And that hurts. It hurts so, so much because I'm not doing it on purpose. I'm not trying to be a flake or a bad partner. I just... I lose track of things, or I get restless and abandon what I'm doing, and before I know it, I've let someone down again. It's like I'm constantly having to apologize, both to my boss at the office and to my wife at home, just trying to make up for all the things I didn't finish. So, yeah, it definitely follows me home. It never really turns off.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient mentions that his manager specifically noted his 'lack of attention to detail' in a formal performance review.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes starting chores like fixing a drawer but failing to finish them, leading his wife to say she cannot count on him to 'follow through.'
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states that he will get 'distracted by something in the garage' while trying to complete a task.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient reports frequently forgetting daily activities and errands, such as picking up the dry cleaning or paying the water bill.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes getting 'restless' and abandoning the tasks he is currently doing.
